extracted.intended_audience: medical researchers, journal editors, press officers, and health journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and empirical findings for evaluating press releases (and subsequent news coverage) of randomized controlled trials, focusing on the presence of 'spin' and factors that lead to misinterpretation of trial results. Includes definition and classification of types of spin, measurable press-release features, and an interpretation/misinterpretation scoring approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'spin'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Spin" defined as a specific reporting (intentional or unintentional) that emphasizes the beneficial effect of the experimental treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition when screening abstracts, press releases, and news items. The study adapted a prior classification originally developed for trials with nonstatistically significant primary outcomes and applied it to all RCTs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of 'spin' to detect
rubrics_metrics.description: Classified types include: a focus on statistically significant results (within-group comparisons, secondary outcomes, subgroup analyses, modified population of analyses); interpretation of statistically nonsignificant primary outcomes as showing treatment equivalence or comparable effectiveness; inadequate claim of safety; inappropriate extrapolation; and failure to acknowledge nonstatistically significant primary outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding text, look for explicit emphasis on secondary/subgroup/within-group significant findings over the primary outcome, wording that treats p>0.05 as equivalence, definitive safety claims without evidence, extrapolation beyond studied population, or omission of nonsignificant primary outcome results. Examples and exemplars are provided in the article's figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release should provide basic information and access to the article
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release should provide journalists with the basic information needed to develop a news story and should ideally provide easy access to the research article (direct link or full reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the press release includes a direct link or full citation; lack of access impedes accurate reporting. The study reports only ~50% provided easy access, flagging this as a quality metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report funding source
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should report the funding source of the RCT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit funding disclosure in the press release; in the study only 36% reported funding. Funding disclosure is relevant to assessing potential bias or promotional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report primary outcomes with numeric results when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Results for primary outcomes should be reported with quantitative detail (not only words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding distinguished releases that reported primary outcomes with words only (41% in this sample). Best practice: include numerical effect sizes, measures of uncertainty, or clear statements about statistical significance rather than vague verbal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention and quantify safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should mention safety/adverse events and, where appropriate, quantify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of safety mention and whether safety is quantified. In the sample, safety was mentioned in 34% and quantified in 20% — lack of safety detail is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report study limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should report study limitations or caveats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only 14% of releases reported limitations in this sample; omission of limitations is an indicator of over-optimistic framing and potential 'spin.' Include explicit limitations or calls for caution where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include balanced quotations; avoid promotional emphasis in quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from authors/editors should moderate claims (e.g., 'further investigation is needed') rather than use emphatic promotional language (e.g., 'this paves the way').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code whether quotations report results with emphasis versus moderation. The study found many quotes used emphasis; best practice is to use measured, contextualized quotes and avoid hyperbole that promotes spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare author/source of the press release
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who wrote or issued the press release (press officer, journal, institution, industry, authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record author/source; the study analyzed press-officer vs other authors as a variable (no association with spin found), but transparency about the source helps assess potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overinterpretation (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid interpreting nonstatistically significant primary outcomes as evidence of equivalence or making inappropriate extrapolations and definitive claims of efficacy/safety unsupported by primary outcome data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for phrases that equate lack of significance with no difference, assert generalizability beyond the study population, or minimize harms. Such language qualifies as 'spin' and is associated with overestimation of benefit in press releases and news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation scoring scale (1–5) for treatment recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1–5 scale to interpret RCT results: 1=definitely get the experimental treatment, 2=probably get it, 3=neutral/decide for yourself, 4=probably not get it, 5=definitely not get it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this scale to rate the message conveyed by the full article, the press release, and the news item independently. Ratings 1–2 = considered beneficial; 3 = neutral; 4–5 = not beneficial. The study used blinded assessors and consensus pair ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinterpretation is defined as the interpretation of the press release or news item differing from that based on the full-text article by at least one class according to the three-class system (beneficial / neutral / not beneficial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify misinterpretation as overestimation (press release/news rates treatment more beneficial than full article) or underestimation. The study flagged a misinterpretation when the source’s classification differed by ≥1 category from the full-text-based classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding and independent review for subjective coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective items (e.g., type of 'spin', interpretation) should be coded by two independent reviewers with discrepancies resolved by consensus; assessments of press releases/news should be blinded to other sources where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study blinded assessors to authors/journal/content of other sources when rating each source. They reported mean kappa for 'spin' = 0.56 (range 0.43–0.69), suggesting moderate agreement; use independent dual coding for reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider predictors associated with 'spin' and overestimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical factors associated with 'spin' and overestimation include: presence of 'spin' in the article abstract conclusions (strongest predictor), publication in a specialized journal, and small sample size; funding source and author of press release were not associated in this study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating risk of spin or likelihood of overestimation from a press release/news item, examine whether the article abstract itself contains spin (the main associated factor: multivariable RR=5.6), whether the trial was in a specialty journal, and whether the sample size is small (<112 in this sample). Use these predictors to prioritize scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect news coverage to mirror press release/abstract spin
rubrics_metrics.description: News items frequently reproduce the same type of 'spin' as present in the press release and article abstract conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the sample of 41 RCTs with news items, 51% of news items contained spin and most mirrored the abstract/press-release spin. Evaluate media coverage for verbatim reproductions of spin and for amplified emphasis.
